content: Telecommunications Relay Service (TRS), also referred to as Relay Service or IP-Relay, is an operator-assisted communication service that enables individuals who are Deaf, Hard of Hearing, Speech-Disabled, or DeafBlind to make telephone calls to standard telephone users. This is achieved through the use of devices such as TDD (TTY), personal computers, or other assistive telephone technologies. Types of Services Available Relay services offer various call types depending on the technical and physical abilities of the users. TTY to Voice / Voice to TTY The most common type of TRS call involves a Deaf individual using a TTY device to communicate with a Hearing individual who can speak and hear. In this setup, typed messages from the TTY user are converted into spoken messages by a TRS operator (also known as a Communication Assistant, Relay Operator, or Relay Agent) and vice versa. This allows individuals who cannot use a standard telephone to communicate with those who can. During the call, it is customary for the Hearing person to say Go Ahead (GA) to indicate it is the TTY user's turn to respond, and Stop Keying (SK) or Ready to hang up when ending the call. Voice Carry Over (VCO) Voice Carry Over (VCO) is another common call type. It allows individuals who are Hard of Hearing or Deaf but can speak to use their voice while receiving responses from a Hearing person via the operator's typed text. Variations of VCO include 2-Line VCO and VCO with Privacy. VCO with Privacy In this variation, the operator does not hear the VCO user's spoken messages. The VCO user does not need to voice GA because they can type it or press a VCO GA button on their device. The Hearing person must still say GA to signal the operator that it is the VCO user's turn. 2-Line VCO This method allows a VCO user to use a TTY or computer to call a TRS operator, who then calls the VCO user on a second telephone line, which serves as the voice line. The user can initiate a three-way call with the Hearing person. This setup is often used by individuals who are Hard of Hearing and prefer to use their residual hearing without needing to say Go Ahead. Both the VCO user and the Hearing person can interrupt each other during the call. However, VCO with Privacy cannot be used with 2-Line VCO due to the three-way call setup. Hearing Carry Over (HCO) Hearing Carry Over (HCO) is less common and is designed for individuals who are Speech-Disabled but can hear. It allows them to listen to the Hearing person's responses while sending their own responses via typed text. The operator voices the HCO user's typed messages, and the HCO user listens to the responses. Variations include 2-Line HCO and HCO with Privacy. HCO with Privacy In this variation, the operator does not hear the Hearing person's spoken messages. The Speech-Disabled user must type GA to signal the operator that it is the Hearing person's turn. The Hearing person does not need to voice GA because the HCO user can hear when the Hearing person finishes speaking. 2-Line HCO Similar to 2-Line VCO, this method allows an HCO user to use a TTY or computer to call a TRS operator, who then calls the HCO user on a second telephone line. The user can initiate a three-way call with the Hearing person. This setup is often used by Speech-Disabled individuals who prefer to use their residual speech without typing GA. Both the HCO user and the Hearing person can interrupt each other during the call. Speech-to-Speech (STS) Speech-to-Speech (STS) is a service for individuals with speech disabilities. A specially trained STS operator revoices what the Speech-Disabled person says to ensure clarity. STS is often combined with VCO for Deaf individuals with partially understandable speech or with 2-Line HCO users. It enables Speech-Disabled individuals to call others, including able-bodied speakers and other Speech-Disabled individuals. It also allows Hearing individuals to call Speech-Disabled individuals. STS is available in countries like Australia, New Zealand, and parts of Sweden. Many STS users have conditions such as Parkinson's disease, cerebral palsy, ALS, multiple sclerosis, muscular dystrophy, or have experienced a stroke. Others may stutter or have undergone a laryngectomy. STS also supports users of speech synthesizers and Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) devices, which can be placed next to a speakerphone for independent communication. DeafBlind Variation Telebraille is a service for DeafBlind individuals, utilizing a TTY with a braille or regular keyboard and a refreshable braille display or Large Visual Display (LVD). The text transmission speed is often reduced to accommodate the user's ability to comprehend moving braille or large print. Telebraille relay operators must be familiar with braille contractions. Some TTY users with mobility disabilities may prefer Telebraille due to its smaller keyboard, regardless of visual impairment. Captioned Telephone Captioned telephones (CapTel) are designed for individuals who are Hard of Hearing, Oral Deaf, or Late-Deafened. These devices display real-time captions of the conversation on a screen embedded in the telephone base. CapTel can also function as a VCO device by switching to VCO mode for direct communication with an HCO user without relay. CapTel systems use a stenographic mask system for voice recognition, similar to live TV closed captioning. Unlike other relay services, CapTel is only available in states that include it as part of their relay service. A variation, 2-Line CapTel, allows users to toggle captions on and off during a call and can be used with other relay services, such as STS for Speech-Disabled users. CapTel USB enables Blind or Low-Vision users to connect to a computer for large print or braille captions. Internet Relay Service Internet relay services replace TTY and telephone lines with specialized computer programs and internet connections. These services include Java-based programs and instant messaging platforms. However, due to the inability to identify the caller's exact location, operators must request the caller's address when making emergency 911 calls. Video Relay Service (VRS) Video Relay Service (VRS) allows individuals who use sign language to communicate via a video interpreter (VI). The VI uses a webcam or videophone to interpret the Deaf or Speech-Disabled person's signs into spoken words for the Hearing person and vice versa. Accessibility and Fraudulent Use TRS systems, particularly internet relay services, are accessible to anyone with the proper equipment, including those without hearing or speech disabilities. This open structure has led to misuse, such as fraudulent calls and prank calls. In response, the FCC has implemented measures to combat abuse, including gathering feedback from relay providers. However, the principle of transparency ensures that relay services remain as easy to use as a standard telephone, without requiring verification of the user's need for assistance.
